chunks: "The main ways are: put a meter in series, put a small sense resistor in series and measure the voltage across it, or sense the magnetic field around the wire without breaking the circuit.
The simplest is a multimeter in current mode, which is accurate at DC but you have to break the circuit, it adds burden voltage, and it only gives an average.
A shunt resistor is the workhorse: I measure the voltage across it with a DMM, a scope or a current-sense amplifier into an ADC.
With a 10 milliohm shunt, one amp gives 10 millivolts and 10 milliwatts of loss.
The trade-off is signal versus loss: a bigger resistor gives more signal but drops more voltage and burns more power, and a tiny one gets buried in amplifier offset.
When I can't break the circuit or need isolation, I'd use a clamp-on or a current probe.
Hall-effect probes work at DC and AC, Rogowski coils work for AC and large currents, and current transformers for AC only. On boards you can use Hall-effect sensor ICs.
Another trick is to use the DC resistance of the inductor, if you filter it properly.
So I choose based on the current range, whether it is DC, how fast it changes, how much voltage I can afford to lose, whether I need isolation, and the accuracy needed."
